reminder: The Einstein tensor of a metric is its Ricci tensor minus half the scalar curvature times the metric.
definition: For a [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold) $(X,g)$ with [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) $\mathrm{Ric}$ and [scalar curvature](c:scalar-curvature) $R$, the Einstein tensor is the symmetric [tensor](c:tensor) field $G=\mathrm{Ric}-\tfrac12 R\,g$. Its divergence is zero by the contracted Bianchi identity.
examples: On a Ricci-flat manifold both $\mathrm{Ric}$ and $R$ are zero, so $G=0$.
In dimension 2 the Einstein tensor is zero for every metric, because $\mathrm{Ric}=\tfrac12 R\,g$ there.
Non-example: the Ricci tensor alone is not the Einstein tensor; its divergence is half the differential of $R$, so it is not divergence free in general.

reminder: A class of structures is elementary when it is the class of all models of one first-order theory.
definition: Fix a [signature](c:signature-in-logic). A class $K$ of [structures](c:structure-in-model-theory) of this signature is elementary if there is a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) $T$ such that $K$ consists exactly of the [models](c:model) of $T$. In other words, a set of first-order sentences axiomatizes $K$.
examples: The class of all groups is elementary: the group axioms are first-order sentences in the signature $(\cdot,e,{}^{-1})$.
The class of algebraically closed fields is elementary: add, for each degree $n\ge1$, one sentence that says every monic polynomial of degree $n$ has a root.
Non-example: the class of finite groups is not elementary, because a first-order theory with arbitrarily large finite models also has an infinite model, by compactness.

steps: Take an elementary class $K$, the class of models of a first-order theory $T$.
Order the models of $T$ by the elementary substructure relation $\preceq$.
The pair $(K,\preceq)$ satisfies the axioms of an abstract elementary class, so each elementary class gives one.
links.why: Results about abstract elementary classes then apply to every first-order theory, and the extra first-order axioms give stronger tools such as compactness.

reminder: Equivariant cohomology of a $G$-space $X$ is the cohomology of the homotopy quotient $EG\times_G X$.
definition: Let a group $G$ act on a space $X$, and let $EG\to BG$ be the universal principal $G$-bundle over the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$. The equivariant cohomology of $X$ is $H^*_G(X)=H^*(EG\times_G X)$, the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the [homotopy quotient](c:homotopy-quotient) of $X$ by the [group action](c:group-action).
examples: For a point $X=\mathrm{pt}$ it gives $H^*(BG)$, the cohomology of the classifying space.
If $G$ acts freely on a nice space $X$, then $H^*_G(X)\cong H^*(X/G)$.

Non-example: the cohomology of the orbit space $X/G$ is not equivariant cohomology in general; for $G=\mathbb Z/2$ acting on a point, $X/G$ is a point but $BG=\mathbb{RP}^\infty$ has nonzero mod 2 cohomology in every degree.

steps: Take the trivial group $G=1$ acting on a space $X$.
Then $EG$ is a point, so $EG\times_G X$ is just $X$.
Hence $H^*_G(X)$ equals the ordinary cohomology $H^*(X)$.
links.why: Every statement about ordinary cohomology is the trivial-group case of a statement about equivariant cohomology.

reminder: A map is equivariant when it carries the action on its source to the action on its target.
definition: Let a monoid $M$ act on a set $X$, let a monoid $N$ act on a set $Y$, and let $\varphi\colon M\to N$ be a map, usually a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism). A function $f\colon X\to Y$ is $\varphi$-equivariant if $f(m\cdot x)=\varphi(m)\cdot f(x)$ for all $m\in M$ and $x\in X$. When $M=N$ and $\varphi$ is the identity, one says only that $f$ is equivariant for the [group action](c:group-action).
examples: A linear map $T\colon V\to W$ between two representations of $G$ with $T(gv)=gT(v)$ is equivariant; it is an [intertwiner](c:intertwiner).
The quotient map $G\to G/H$ is equivariant for the actions of $G$ by left multiplication.
Non-example: let $\mathbb Z$ act on itself by translation and take $f(x)=x^2$ with $\varphi=\mathrm{id}$; then $f(1+1)=4$ but $1+f(1)=2$.

steps: Take two linear representations $V$ and $W$ of $G$ and an intertwiner $T\colon V\to W$.
A representation is an action of $G$ on the underlying set of the vector space.
The intertwining condition $T(gv)=gT(v)$ is the equivariance condition with $\varphi=\mathrm{id}$.
links.why: Intertwiners are the equivariant maps that are also linear, so general results on equivariant maps apply to them.

reminder: An even number is an integer that is divisible by 2.
definition: An [integer](c:integer) $n$ is even if $n=2k$ for some integer $k$, that is, if $2$ divides $n$ (see [divisibility](c:divisibility)). Equivalently, $n$ leaves remainder $0$ when divided by $2$.
examples: The number $6$ is even because $6=2\cdot 3$.
The number $0$ is even because $0=2\cdot 0$, and $-4$ is even because $-4=2\cdot(-2)$.
Non-example: the number $7$ is not even, because $7=2\cdot 3+1$ leaves remainder $1$.

reminder: A strategy is evolutionarily stable when a population that plays it resists invasion by any small group of mutants.
definition: Take a symmetric two-player game in which a player who uses $s$ against $t$ gets the payoff $u(s,t)$. A [strategy](c:mixed-strategy) $s^*$ is evolutionarily stable if, for every strategy $t\neq s^*$, either $u(s^*,s^*)>u(t,s^*)$, or $u(s^*,s^*)=u(t,s^*)$ and $u(s^*,t)>u(t,t)$. The first case is a strict [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium); in the second case $s^*$ must also do better against $t$ than $t$ does against itself.
examples: In the Hawk-Dove game with prize $V$ smaller than the cost $C$ of a fight, the mixed strategy that plays Hawk with probability $V/C$ is evolutionarily stable.
In the Prisoner's Dilemma, always defecting is evolutionarily stable, because it is a strict best reply to itself.
Non-example: in Rock-Paper-Scissors with payoffs $1$, $-1$ and $0$, the uniform mixed strategy is a Nash equilibrium. It is not evolutionarily stable, because it only ties against a pure mutant.

steps: Take an evolutionarily stable strategy $s^*$ of a symmetric game.
In both cases of the definition, $u(s^*,s^*)\ge u(t,s^*)$ holds for every strategy $t$.
So $s^*$ is a best reply to itself, and the pair $(s^*,s^*)$ is a symmetric Nash equilibrium.
A symmetric Nash equilibrium is evolutionarily stable only if it also does better against every tying mutant than the mutant does against itself.
links.why: Every evolutionarily stable strategy gives a Nash equilibrium, so equilibrium results apply, and the extra condition removes unstable equilibria.

reminder: An exponential field is a field with a map from its additive group to its multiplicative group that turns sums into products.
definition: An exponential field is a [field](c:field) $K$ together with a map $E\colon K\to K^\times$ with $E(x+y)=E(x)E(y)$ for all $x,y\in K$; that is, a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) from $(K,+)$ to $(K^\times,\cdot)$. In an ordered exponential field, $K$ is an [ordered field](c:ordered-field) and $E$ is also strictly increasing.
examples: The real numbers with $E(x)=e^x$ form an ordered exponential field; this is the real exponential field of Wilkie's theorem.
The complex numbers with $E(z)=e^z$ form an exponential field; here $E$ is not injective, because $e^{2\pi i}=1$.
Non-example: on $\mathbb R$ the map $x\mapsto x^2$ is not an exponential, because $(1+1)^2=4$ differs from $1^2\cdot 1^2=1$, and it takes the value $0$.

reminder: The group $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$ is the $n$-th cohomology of $\mathrm{Hom}_R(P_\bullet,B)$ for a projective resolution $P_\bullet$ of $A$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring) and let $A,B$ be [modules](c:module) over $R$. Choose a [projective resolution](c:has-projective-resolution) $\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to A$ and apply $\mathrm{Hom}_R(-,B)$ to it to get a cochain complex. The group $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$ is the $n$-th [cohomology](c:cohomology) of this complex; it does not depend on the resolution.
examples: $\mathrm{Ext}^0_R(A,B)=\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,B)$.
$\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/n,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/n$, computed with the resolution $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n$.
If $A$ is projective, then $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)=0$ for all $n\ge1$.
Non-example: $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/n,\mathbb Z/n)\cong\mathbb Z/n$ is a [Tor group](c:tor-functor); it comes from tensoring a resolution, not from applying $\mathrm{Hom}$.

steps: Take the left exact functor $F=\mathrm{Hom}_R(A,-)$ on $R$-modules.
Its $n$-th right derived functor $R^nF$ is computed from an injective resolution of the second argument $B$.
The value $R^nF(B)$ is $\mathrm{Ext}^n_R(A,B)$, and a balancing argument shows that a projective resolution of $A$ gives the same groups.
links.why: A learner can use the general machinery of derived functors, such as long exact sequences, for Ext groups.

reminder: A functor is faithful when it sends different parallel morphisms to different morphisms.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ is faithful if, for all objects $x,y$ of the [category](c:category) $\mathcal C$, the map $\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)$ on hom-sets is injective. So $f\neq g$ with the same source and target implies $Ff\neq Fg$.
examples: The forgetful functor from groups to sets is faithful, because a homomorphism is determined by its underlying function.
The inclusion functor of any subcategory is faithful.
Non-example: view a nontrivial group $G$ as a one-object category. The functor to the terminal category is not faithful, because it sends every element of $G$ to the identity.

steps: Take a fully faithful functor $F$.
On each hom-set the map of $F$ is a bijection.
A bijection is injective, so $F$ is faithful.
Fullness, the surjectivity of this map, is the extra condition of a fully faithful functor.
links.why: Faithfulness is the injectivity half of fully faithful, so a learner can check the two halves separately.

reminder: The Farey sequence $F_n$ lists the fractions in lowest terms in $[0,1]$ with denominator at most $n$ in increasing order.
definition: The Farey sequence $F_n$ of order $n$ is the increasing sequence of all [rational numbers](c:rational-number) $a/b$ with $0\le a/b\le 1$, $1\le b\le n$ and $a,b$ [coprime](c:coprime-integers). Some authors do not restrict the fractions to $[0,1]$.
examples: Non-example: $2/4$ never occurs in a Farey sequence, because it is not in lowest terms; the fraction $1/2$ occurs instead.

reminder: A finite abelian group is a group that has finitely many elements and a commutative operation.
definition: A finite abelian group is a [group](c:group) that is both [finite](c:finite-group) and [abelian](c:abelian-group): it has finitely many elements, and $ab=ba$ for all elements $a,b$. By the structure theorem, every finite abelian group is a direct product of cyclic groups of prime power order.
examples: The group $\mathbb Z/n$ is finite abelian for every $n\ge1$.
The group $\mathbb Z/2\times\mathbb Z/2$ is finite abelian, and it is not cyclic.
Non-example: the symmetric group $S_3$ is finite but not abelian, and $\mathbb Z$ is abelian but not finite.

steps: Start with a finite abelian group $G$.
Forget the condition $ab=ba$.
What remains is a finite group, so $G$ is a special case; the converse fails for $S_3$.
links.why: Results about finite groups apply to finite abelian groups, and commutativity adds tools such as the structure theorem.

steps: Start with a finite abelian group $G$.
Forget that $G$ has finitely many elements.
What remains is an abelian group, so $G$ is a special case; the converse fails for $\mathbb Z$.
links.why: Results about abelian groups apply to finite abelian groups, and finiteness adds counting tools such as Lagrange's theorem.

reminder: A Fréchet algebra is a complete algebra whose topology comes from countably many submultiplicative seminorms.
definition: A Fréchet algebra is a complex [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) $A$ with a countable family of [seminorms](c:seminorm) $p_k$ that separates points and satisfies $p_k(ab)\le p_k(a)p_k(b)$. The algebra $A$ must be complete in the topology of these seminorms, so it is a [Fréchet space](c:frechet-space) with continuous multiplication.
examples: The algebra $\mathcal O(X)$ of holomorphic functions on a Stein manifold $X$, with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets, is a Fréchet algebra.
The algebra of smooth functions on the circle, with seminorms that bound each derivative, is a Fréchet algebra.
Non-example: the algebra $\mathbb C[x]$ with the supremum norm on $[0,1]$ is a normed algebra but it is not complete, so it is not a Fréchet algebra.

steps: Take a Banach algebra $B$ with a submultiplicative norm $\|\cdot\|$.
Use the constant sequence $p_k=\|\cdot\|$ as the countable family of submultiplicative seminorms.
A Banach space is complete and metrizable, so $B$ is a Fréchet algebra.
links.why: Facts about Fréchet algebras apply to Banach algebras, and examples such as algebras of holomorphic functions go beyond normed algebras.

steps: Take a Fréchet algebra $A$.
Its multiplication is continuous for the topology of the seminorms.
So $A$ is a topological algebra, with the extra conditions that the topology is locally convex, metrizable and complete.
links.why: General facts about topological algebras apply to Fréchet algebras, and the extra conditions give tools such as the open mapping theorem.

reminder: The free loop space of $X$ is the space of all continuous maps from the circle to $X$.
definition: The free loop space $\mathcal LX$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is the set of all continuous maps $S^1\to X$, with no fixed base point, with the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology). Evaluation at the base point of the [circle](c:circle) gives a map $\mathcal LX\to X$ whose fibre over $x_0$ is the based [loop space](c:loop-space) $\Omega X$.
examples: If $X$ is contractible, then $\mathcal LX$ is contractible.

For a discrete group $G$, the free loop space of the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) $BG$ is $\coprod_{[g]}BC_G(g)$, with one piece for each conjugacy class $[g]$ and its centralizer $C_G(g)$.
Non-example: the based loop space $\Omega X$ holds only the loops through the fixed point $x_0$, so it is a subspace of $\mathcal LX$ and in general not equal to it.

steps: Work in the $(\infty,1)$-category of spaces, and take a space $X$.
The free loop space object of $X$ is the homotopy pullback $X\times_{X\times X}X$ of the diagonal with itself.
In spaces, this homotopy pullback is the space $\mathcal LX$ of free loops.
links.why: The free loop space of a space is the model of a construction that makes sense in every $(\infty,1)$-category.

reminder: A functor of $(\infty,1)$-categories is fully faithful when it induces an equivalence on every hom-space.
definition: A functor $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ between [(∞,1)-categories](c:infinity-1-category) is fully faithful if, for all objects $x,y$ of $\mathcal C$, the induced map of hom-spaces $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(x,y)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(Fx,Fy)$ is an equivalence of [∞-groupoids](c:infinity-groupoid). In the model of quasi-categories, these hom-spaces are [hom-objects](c:hom-object-in-a-quasi-category).
examples: The inclusion of sets, as discrete $\infty$-groupoids, into all $\infty$-groupoids is fully faithful.
The Yoneda embedding of an $(\infty,1)$-category into its presheaves is fully faithful.
Non-example: for a nontrivial group $G$, the inclusion of a point into the groupoid $BG$ is not fully faithful. The hom-space of the point is a point, but that of $BG$ is the set $G$.

steps: Take a fully faithful functor $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ of ordinary categories.
View each category as an $(\infty,1)$-category whose hom-spaces are discrete sets.
A bijection of sets is an equivalence of discrete spaces, so $F$ is fully faithful as a functor of $(\infty,1)$-categories.
links.why: A learner can read the new notion as the old one, with bijections on hom-sets replaced by equivalences of hom-spaces.

reminder: A fundamental unit of a real quadratic field is a unit greater than 1 that generates all units up to sign.
definition: Let $K$ be a [real quadratic field](c:real-quadratic-field) with [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal O_K$. The [group of units](c:group-of-units) of $\mathcal O_K$ is $\{\pm\varepsilon^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$ for a unique unit $\varepsilon>1$, and this $\varepsilon$ is the fundamental unit of $K$. Equivalently, it is the smallest unit of $\mathcal O_K$ that is greater than 1.
examples: In $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ the fundamental unit is $1+\sqrt2$.
In $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ the fundamental unit is $2+\sqrt3$, because $2^2-3\cdot1^2=1$ (see the [Pell equation](c:pell-equation)).
Non-example: $3+2\sqrt2$ is a unit of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ greater than 1, but it equals $(1+\sqrt2)^2$, so it is not fundamental.

reminder: A game on the unit square is a two-player zero-sum game in which each player picks a number in $[0,1]$.
definition: A game on the unit square is a [zero-sum game](c:zero-sum-game) in which player I chooses $x$ and player II chooses $y$, both in the [unit interval](c:closed-interval) $[0,1]$. Then II pays I the amount $K(x,y)$ for a given payoff function $K\colon[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$. The players may also use [mixed strategies](c:mixed-strategy), which are probability measures on $[0,1]$, and the payoff is then the expected value of $K$.
examples: For $K(x,y)=(x-y)^2$, player I does best by picking $0$ or $1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each. Player II does best by picking $y=\tfrac12$, and the value of the game is $\tfrac14$.
For $K(x,y)=x-y$, the best choices are $x=1$ and $y=1$, and the value of the game is $0$.
Non-example: a matrix game with two rows and three columns is not a game on the unit square, because the choice sets are finite.

steps: Take a two-player zero-sum game.
Let the set of pure strategies of each player be the interval $[0,1]$.
The payoff is then a function $K(x,y)$ on the unit square, and this is a game on the unit square.
links.why: Minimax ideas for zero-sum games carry over, but infinite strategy sets need extra conditions such as continuity of $K$.

reminder: A generalized quaternion group is a non-abelian group of order $2^n$ with exactly one element of order 2.
definition: For $n\ge3$ the generalized quaternion group $Q_{2^n}$ is the [group](c:group) of order $2^n$ with presentation $\langle x,y\mid x^{2^{n-1}}=1,\ y^2=x^{2^{n-2}},\ y^{-1}xy=x^{-1}\rangle$. It has a [cyclic subgroup](c:cyclic-subgroup) $\langle x\rangle$ of index 2, and for $n=3$ it is the [quaternion group](c:quaternion-group) of order 8.
examples: The group $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ is the case $n=3$.
The group $Q_{16}$ has order 16, with $x$ of order 8 and with the unique involution $x^4$.
Non-example: the [dihedral group of order 8](c:dihedral-group-of-order-8) is non-abelian of order $2^3$, but it has five involutions, so it is not generalized quaternion.

steps: Take $n=3$ in the presentation of $Q_{2^n}$.
Then $x$ has order 4, $y^2=x^2$ and $y^{-1}xy=x^{-1}$.
These are the relations of the quaternion group $Q_8$ with $x=i$ and $y=j$.
links.why: Facts about $Q_8$, such as its unique involution, extend to the whole family.

steps: Take $Q_{2^n}$, a group of order $2^n$.
The order is a power of the prime 2, so every element has 2-power order.
So $Q_{2^n}$ is a 2-group, a special case of a $p$-group.
links.why: Results on $p$-groups, such as a nontrivial center, apply to generalized quaternion groups.

reminder: A harmonic brick is a box whose integer side lengths $a_1\mid a_2\mid\cdots\mid a_n$ each divide the next.
definition: A brick is a rectangular box in $\mathbb R^n$ with side lengths $a_1,\dots,a_n$. It is harmonic if all $a_i$ are positive integers and each side length [divides](c:divisibility) the next, $a_1\mid a_2\mid\cdots\mid a_n$.
examples: The $1\times2\times6$ brick is harmonic, because $1\mid2\mid6$.
The $1\times2\times4\times8$ brick is harmonic, and so is every cube with integer side length.
Non-example: the $2\times3\times6$ brick is not harmonic, because $2$ does not divide $3$.

reminder: The Henstock-Kurzweil integral is the limit of Riemann sums over tagged partitions that are fine for a gauge.
definition: A function $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable with integral $I$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a gauge $\delta\colon[a,b]\to(0,\infty)$ such that $\bigl|\sum_i f(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})-I\bigr|<\varepsilon$ for every [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) with $[x_{i-1},x_i]\subset(t_i-\delta(t_i),t_i+\delta(t_i))$. The [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) is the case of a constant gauge.
examples: Every Riemann integrable function is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable with the same integral.
If $F$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, then $F'$ is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable with integral $F(b)-F(a)$, even when $F'$ is not Lebesgue integrable, as for $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ with $F(0)=0$.
Non-example: the function $f(x)=1/x$ with $f(0)=0$ is not Henstock-Kurzweil integrable on $[0,1]$, because $\int_\varepsilon^1f$ tends to infinity as $\varepsilon\to0$.

steps: Take a Riemann integrable function $f$ on $[a,b]$ with integral $I$, and let $\varepsilon>0$.
Choose $\eta>0$ such that all tagged partitions with mesh below $\eta$ have Riemann sums within $\varepsilon$ of $I$.
Take the constant gauge $\delta=\eta/3$; every $\delta$-fine tagged partition then has mesh below $\eta$.
So $f$ is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable with the same integral $I$.
links.why: The gauge integral keeps every Riemann integral and also integrates every derivative, so the fundamental theorem of calculus needs no extra conditions.

reminder: A Hermitian symmetric space is a Hermitian manifold in which every point is an isolated fixed point of a holomorphic involutive isometry.
definition: A Hermitian symmetric space is a connected [Hermitian manifold](c:hermitian-manifold) $M$ such that every point $p$ is an isolated fixed point of an involutive holomorphic [isometry](c:isometry) $s_p\colon M\to M$, the symmetry at $p$. Such a space is a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) and a [symmetric space](c:symmetric-space).
examples: Complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the Fubini-Study metric is a Hermitian symmetric space.
The open unit disc with the hyperbolic metric is a Hermitian symmetric space, and so is the Siegel upper half-space.
Non-example: the sphere $S^4$ is a symmetric space but it has no complex structure, so it is not a Hermitian symmetric space.

steps: Take a Hermitian symmetric space $M$ with its fundamental form $\omega$ and a point $p$.
The symmetry $s_p$ acts as $-1$ on $T_pM$, so it acts as $-1$ on 3-forms at $p$.
The form $\omega$ is invariant under $s_p$, so $d\omega$ is invariant too, and it vanishes at $p$.
As $p$ is arbitrary, $d\omega=0$, so $M$ is a Kähler manifold.
links.why: Kähler geometry applies to every Hermitian symmetric space, and the symmetries add strong homogeneity.

steps: Take a Hermitian symmetric space $M$ with its symmetries $s_p$.
Each $s_p$ is an involutive isometry with isolated fixed point $p$, so $M$ is a symmetric space.
The added conditions are a compatible complex structure and the holomorphy of every symmetry.
links.why: The Lie-theoretic description of symmetric spaces applies, and the complex structure adds tools such as bounded domain realizations.

reminder: A bounded operator $T$ is Hilbert-Schmidt when $\sum\|Te_i\|^2$ is finite for an orthonormal basis $(e_i)$.
definition: A [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) $T\colon H\to K$ between [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space) is Hilbert-Schmidt if $\|T\|_{HS}^2=\sum_i\|Te_i\|^2<\infty$ for an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $(e_i)$ of $H$. This sum does not depend on the choice of basis, and the Hilbert-Schmidt operators form a Hilbert space with the norm $\|T\|_{HS}$.
examples: The diagonal operator $Te_n=e_n/n$ on $\ell^2$ is Hilbert-Schmidt, because $\sum_n 1/n^2$ is finite.
An integral operator on $L^2([0,1])$ with kernel $k\in L^2([0,1]^2)$ is Hilbert-Schmidt, and $\|T\|_{HS}=\|k\|_{L^2}$.
Non-example: the identity operator on $\ell^2$ is not Hilbert-Schmidt, because $\sum_n\|e_n\|^2$ is infinite.

steps: Let $H$ be separable with orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, take a Hilbert-Schmidt operator $T$, and let $P_N$ project onto $\mathrm{span}(e_1,\dots,e_N)$.
The operators $TP_N$ have finite rank.
The norm of $T-TP_N$ is at most $(\sum_{i>N}\|Te_i\|^2)^{1/2}$, which tends to $0$.
A norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact, so $T$ is compact.
links.why: Compact operator theory, such as the spectral theorem, applies to Hilbert-Schmidt operators, which also have a summable-squares norm.

reminder: A holomorphic immersion is a holomorphic map between complex manifolds whose differential is injective at every point.
definition: A holomorphic map $f\colon M\to N$ of [complex manifolds](c:complex-manifold) is a holomorphic immersion if its [differential](c:differential) $df_p\colon T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ is injective at every point $p\in M$. Locally, $f$ then looks like the inclusion of a coordinate subspace $\mathbb C^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^n$.
examples: The inclusion of a complex line into $\mathbb C^2$ is a holomorphic immersion.
The map $z\mapsto e^z$ from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb C$ is a holomorphic immersion, because $e^z\neq0$, although it is not injective.
Non-example: the map $z\mapsto(z^2,z^3)$ from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb C^2$ is holomorphic but not an immersion at $0$, because its derivative $(2z,3z^2)$ vanishes there.

steps: Take a holomorphic immersion $f\colon M\to N$ of complex manifolds.
Forget the complex structures and keep the underlying smooth manifolds.
The map $f$ is smooth and its real differential is injective, so $f$ is an immersion; the added condition is that $f$ is holomorphic.
links.why: Smooth immersion theory, such as local normal forms, applies to holomorphic immersions.

reminder: The $n$-th homotopy group of a spectrum $E$ is the colimit of the groups $\pi_{n+k}(E_k)$ over $k$.
definition: For a [spectrum](c:spectrum-object) $E=(E_k,\sigma_k\colon\Sigma E_k\to E_{k+1})$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$, the homotopy group is $\pi_nE=\operatorname{colim}_k\pi_{n+k}(E_k)$ over large $k$, along the maps given by suspension and $\sigma_k$ on [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group). Equivalently, $\pi_nE=[\mathbb S^n,E]$ in the [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category), where $\mathbb S$ is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum).
examples: For the sphere spectrum $\mathbb S$, the group $\pi_n\mathbb S$ is the $n$-th stable homotopy group of spheres; for example $\pi_0\mathbb S=\mathbb Z$ and $\pi_1\mathbb S=\mathbb Z/2$.
For the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $HA$ of an abelian group $A$, $\pi_0HA=A$ and $\pi_nHA=0$ for $n\neq0$.
Non-example: for a fixed $k$, the group $\pi_{n+k}(E_k)$ is only one term of the colimit, so in general it is not $\pi_nE$.

steps: Take a pointed space $X$ and its suspension spectrum $\Sigma^\infty X$, which has the spaces $\Sigma^kX$.
The group $\pi_n(\Sigma^\infty X)$ is $\operatorname{colim}_k\pi_{n+k}(\Sigma^kX)$.
This colimit is the stable homotopy group $\pi_n^s(X)$ of the space $X$.
links.why: Stable homotopy groups of spaces are the special case of spectrum homotopy groups for suspension spectra.

reminder: An extension $B\subseteq E$ is Hopf-Galois when the canonical map $E\otimes_BE\to E\otimes H$ is bijective.
definition: Let $H$ be a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) over a field $k$, and let $E$ be a right $H$-[comodule algebra](c:comodule-algebra) with coaction $\rho\colon E\to E\otimes H$. Let $B=\{e\in E:\rho(e)=e\otimes1\}$ be the subalgebra of coinvariants. The extension $B\subseteq E$ is $H$-Galois if the canonical map $E\otimes_BE\to E\otimes H$, $x\otimes y\mapsto\sum xy_{(0)}\otimes y_{(1)}$, is bijective.
examples: A finite [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) $L/K$ with group $G$ is $H$-Galois for $H=K^G$, the Hopf algebra of $K$-valued functions on $G$.
A Hopf algebra $H$ is $H$-Galois over $k$ with its coproduct as coaction, because the antipode inverts the canonical map.
Non-example: for a Hopf algebra $H\neq k$ and the trivial coaction $\rho(e)=e\otimes1$, one has $B=E$ and the canonical map $E\to E\otimes H$ is not surjective.

steps: Take a finite Galois extension $L/K$ with group $G$, and let $H=K^G$ be the Hopf algebra of $K$-valued functions on $G$.
The coaction $\rho(x)=\sum_g g(x)\otimes\delta_g$ makes $L$ an $H$-comodule algebra with coinvariants $K$.
The canonical map $L\otimes_KL\to L\otimes H$ is bijective, which is the Galois condition, so $L/K$ is $H$-Galois.
links.why: Classical Galois theory is the Hopf-Galois theory of the function algebra of the Galois group.

steps: Take a principal $G$-bundle $P\to X$ of affine schemes, where $G$ is an affine group scheme.
Put $E=\mathcal O(P)$, $H=\mathcal O(G)$ and $B=\mathcal O(X)$; the action $P\times G\to P$ gives a coaction $E\to E\otimes H$.
The isomorphism $P\times G\to P\times_XP$ of principal bundles dualizes to $E\otimes_BE\cong E\otimes H$.
links.why: Hopf-Galois extensions are the algebraic form of principal bundles, so they give a meaning to noncommutative principal bundles.

reminder: A hyperbola is the set of points in a plane whose distances to two fixed points differ by a constant.
definition: A hyperbola is the set of points $P$ in the [plane](c:plane) with $\bigl||PF_1|-|PF_2|\bigr|=2a$, for two fixed points $F_1,F_2$ (the foci) at distance $2c$ with $0<a<c$. In suitable coordinates it is the curve $x^2/a^2-y^2/b^2=1$ with $b^2=c^2-a^2$, a [conic section](c:conic-section) with two branches.
examples: The graph of $y=1/x$ is a hyperbola with the foci $(\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$ and $(-\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$.
The curve $x^2-y^2=1$ has the vertices $(\pm1,0)$ and the asymptotes $y=\pm x$.
Non-example: the ellipse $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1$ has a constant sum of distances to its foci, not a constant difference, and it is bounded.

steps: Take a conic section, the curve in which a plane cuts a double cone.
Require that the plane misses the apex and meets both halves of the cone.
The curve then has two branches, and it is a hyperbola.
links.why: Hyperbolas inherit the focus and directrix properties of conics, and the two branches distinguish them from ellipses and parabolas.

reminder: An (∞,1)-topos is hypercomplete when every ∞-connective morphism in it is an equivalence.
definition: An [(∞,1)-topos](c:infinity-1-topos) $\mathcal X$ is hypercomplete if every ∞-connective morphism of $\mathcal X$ is an [equivalence](c:equivalence), where a morphism is ∞-connective if it is [$n$-connective](c:n-connective-object) for every $n$. This is the Whitehead theorem in $\mathcal X$: a morphism that is an isomorphism on all homotopy sheaves is an equivalence.
examples: The $(\infty,1)$-topos of $\infty$-groupoids is hypercomplete; this is the classical Whitehead theorem.
For every small $(\infty,1)$-category $\mathcal C$, the $(\infty,1)$-topos of presheaves of $\infty$-groupoids on $\mathcal C$ is hypercomplete, because equivalences are tested objectwise.
Non-example: the $(\infty,1)$-topos of sheaves of $\infty$-groupoids on the Hilbert cube is not hypercomplete.

steps: Take an $(\infty,1)$-topos $\mathcal X$.
Add the condition that every ∞-connective morphism of $\mathcal X$ is an equivalence.
Such an $\mathcal X$ is hypercomplete, so it satisfies the Whitehead theorem.
links.why: In a hypercomplete topos a morphism is an equivalence if it induces isomorphisms on all homotopy sheaves, so equivalences can be checked on stalks of homotopy.

reminder: An infinite graph is a graph whose set of vertices is infinite.
definition: An infinite graph is a [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ whose vertex set $V$ is an [infinite set](c:infinite-set). Its edges join pairs of vertices as in a finite graph, but a vertex may have infinitely many neighbours.
examples: The two-way infinite path on $\mathbb Z$, with the edges $\{n,n+1\}$, is an infinite graph.
The complete graph on the natural numbers is an infinite graph in which every vertex has infinite degree.
Non-example: a cycle $C_n$ is a [finite graph](c:finite-graph), because it has only $n$ vertices.

steps: Take a graph $G=(V,E)$.
Add the condition that the vertex set $V$ is infinite.
Finite arguments, such as induction on the number of vertices, no longer apply.
links.why: Definitions for graphs still apply, and the infinite case needs new methods.

reminder: An infinitesimal is a number whose absolute value is smaller than every positive real number.
definition: In an [ordered field](c:ordered-field) $F$ that extends the [real numbers](c:real-number), such as the hyperreal numbers, an element $\varepsilon$ is infinitesimal if $|\varepsilon|<r$ for every positive real $r$. The number $0$ is infinitesimal, and a nonzero infinitesimal exists only when $F$ is not [Archimedean](c:archimedean).
examples: In the hyperreal numbers, $1/N$ is a nonzero infinitesimal for every infinite hypernatural number $N$.
In the field $\mathbb R(x)$ of rational functions, ordered so that $x$ is larger than every real number, $1/x$ is a nonzero infinitesimal.
If $\varepsilon,\delta$ are infinitesimal and $b$ is finite, then $\varepsilon+\delta$ and $b\varepsilon$ are infinitesimal.
Non-example: a nonzero real number $r$ is not infinitesimal, because $|r|<|r|/2$ is false.

reminder: An (∞,1)-operad is an operad whose operations form spaces and whose composition is associative and unital up to coherent homotopy.
definition: An (∞,1)-operad is the analogue of an [operad](c:operad) in [(∞,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category) theory. For each arity it has a space of operations, and the composition is associative and unital up to coherent homotopy. One model is a [dendroidal set](c:dendroidal-set) with fillers for inner horns; another is Lurie's ∞-operad, a functor $\mathcal O^\otimes\to N(\mathrm{Fin}_*)$ of ∞-categories.
examples: Every ordinary operad, such as the operad of commutative monoids, gives an (∞,1)-operad with discrete spaces of operations, its dendroidal nerve.
The little $n$-disks operad is an (∞,1)-operad whose spaces of operations are configuration spaces of points in $\mathbb R^n$.
Non-example: a family of spaces $P(n)$ with symmetric group actions but no composition maps is not an (∞,1)-operad.

steps: Take an ordinary operad $P$ with a set of operations $P(n)$ in each arity.
Regard each set as a discrete space, and form the dendroidal nerve $N(P)$.
The nerve $N(P)$ has fillers for inner horns, so it is an (∞,1)-operad whose composition is strict.
links.why: Ordinary operads are the (∞,1)-operads with discrete spaces of operations.

steps: Take an (∞,1)-category $\mathcal C$ and use its objects as the colours.
Let the space of operations from $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ to $y$ be empty unless $n=1$.
For $n=1$ let this space be $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(x_1,y)$, and let composition be that of $\mathcal C$.
links.why: An (∞,1)-category is an (∞,1)-operad with only unary operations, as a category is an operad with only unary operations.

reminder: An (∞,1)-sheaf is a presheaf of ∞-groupoids that satisfies descent for every covering sieve.
definition: Let $(\mathcal C,J)$ be an [(∞,1)-site](c:infinity-1-site). An (∞,1)-sheaf on it is an [(∞,1)-presheaf](c:infinity-1-presheaf) $F\colon\mathcal C^{op}\to\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ such that, for every [covering sieve](c:covering-sieve) $R$ of an object $U$, the map $F(U)\to\lim_{(V\to U)\in R}F(V)$ is an equivalence of [∞-groupoids](c:infinity-groupoid). This is the [descent](c:descent) condition.
examples: Every ordinary sheaf of sets, seen as a presheaf of discrete ∞-groupoids, is an (∞,1)-sheaf.
The assignment of the groupoid of $G$-bundles to each open set of a space is an (∞,1)-sheaf with 1-truncated values.

Non-example: the constant presheaf $U\mapsto\mathbb R$ on a space with two components is not an (∞,1)-sheaf. For the cover by the two components, $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ is not an equivalence.

steps: Take a sheaf of sets $F$ on a site $(\mathcal C,J)$.
View each set $F(U)$ as a discrete ∞-groupoid, so that $F$ is an (∞,1)-presheaf.
Limits of discrete ∞-groupoids are limits of sets, so the sheaf condition for $F$ is the descent condition.
links.why: Ordinary sheaves are the (∞,1)-sheaves with discrete values, so sheaf theory sits inside the higher theory.

reminder: An internal category in $\mathcal E$ is a category whose objects and morphisms are objects of $\mathcal E$, with structure maps in $\mathcal E$.
definition: Let $\mathcal E$ be a [category](c:category) with [pullbacks](c:pullback). An internal category $C$ in $\mathcal E$ consists of objects $C_0$ and $C_1$ of $\mathcal E$ with morphisms $s,t\colon C_1\to C_0$ (source and target), $i\colon C_0\to C_1$ (identities) and $m\colon C_1\times_{C_0}C_1\to C_1$ (composition). These satisfy the axioms of a category as commutative diagrams in $\mathcal E$, which is the idea of [internalization](c:internalization).
examples: An internal category in the category of sets is a small category, with $C_0$ the set of objects and $C_1$ the set of morphisms.
An internal category in the category of topological spaces is a topological category, with continuous structure maps.
An internal category in the category of groups is a [strict 2-group](c:strict-2-group), which is the same as a crossed module.
Non-example: two sets $C_0,C_1$ with source and target maps but no composition $m$ form a graph, not an internal category.

steps: Take $\mathcal E=\mathrm{Set}$, which has all pullbacks.
An internal category in $\mathrm{Set}$ has a set of objects $C_0$ and a set of morphisms $C_1$ with the maps $s,t,i,m$.
The commutative diagrams are the usual category axioms, so it is a small category, and each small category arises this way.
links.why: Small categories are the internal categories in sets, so one definition covers categories in many settings.

steps: Take a groupoid object $G$ in $\mathcal E$ with source, target, identity, composition and inversion maps.
Forget the inversion map $G_1\to G_1$.
The remaining structure satisfies the axioms of an internal category, so each groupoid object is an internal category.
links.why: Internal groupoids are the internal categories whose morphisms have inverses.

reminder: An ordered module is a module with a partial order in which scalar multiplication by nonnegative elements preserves order.
definition: Let $R$ be an [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring), and let $M$ be an $R$-[module](c:module) with a [partial order](c:partial-order) $\le$ such that $M$ is an [ordered abelian group](c:ordered-abelian-group). Then $M$ is an ordered module if $x\le y$ and $r\ge0$ imply $rx\le ry$, and if $v\ge0$ and $r\le s$ imply $rv\le sv$.
examples: The space $\mathbb R^n$ with the coordinatewise order is an ordered module over $\mathbb R$.
Every ordered ring is an ordered module over itself; for example $\mathbb Z$ is an ordered module over $\mathbb Z$.

Non-example: give $\mathbb R$ the order $x\preceq y$ when $y-x\in\mathbb N$; this is a partially ordered abelian group, but not an ordered $\mathbb R$-module, because $0\preceq1$ while $\tfrac12\cdot0\preceq\tfrac12\cdot1$ fails.

steps: Take an ordered abelian group $G$ and use the ordered ring $\mathbb Z$ as scalars.
The $\mathbb Z$-module structure is $n\cdot g=g+\dots+g$ with $n$ summands.
For $n\ge0$ and $g\le h$ we get $ng\le nh$, by adding the inequality $n$ times.
For $g\ge0$ and $m\le n$ we get $mg\le ng$, because $(n-m)g\ge0$.
links.why: Ordered abelian groups are the ordered modules over the integers, so module results apply to them.

reminder: A point of a topological space is isolated when the set containing only that point is open.
definition: A point $P$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is isolated if the singleton $\{P\}$ is open in $X$. Equivalently, some neighbourhood of $P$ contains no other point of $X$, so $P$ is not an [accumulation point](c:accumulation-point) of $X$.
examples: Every point of $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R$ is isolated, because $\{n\}=\mathbb Z\cap(n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)$.
In the set $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}\subset\mathbb R$, every point $1/n$ is isolated.
Non-example: the point $0$ in $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ is not isolated, because every neighbourhood of $0$ contains some $1/n$.

reminder: The join of two maps into $X$ is the induced map to $X$ out of the pushout of their pullback.
definition: Let $f\colon A\to X$ and $g\colon B\to X$ be maps of [homotopy types](c:homotopy-type) with the same codomain. Form the [pullback](c:pullback) $A\times_XB$ and the [pushout](c:pushout) $A*_XB$ of the span $A\leftarrow A\times_XB\to B$. The join $f*g\colon A*_XB\to X$ is the map that $f$ and $g$ induce on this pushout.
examples: If $X$ is a point, then $f*g$ is the map from the usual [join of spaces](c:join-of-topological-spaces) $A*B$ to the point.
If $f=g=\mathrm{id}_X$, then the pullback is $X$, the pushout is $X$, and the join is $\mathrm{id}_X$.
Non-example: the fibre product $A\times_XB$ alone is not the join; it is only the middle of the span whose pushout gives the join.

steps: Take spaces $A$ and $B$ and the maps $f\colon A\to *$ and $g\colon B\to *$ to a point.
The pullback $A\times_*B$ is the product $A\times B$.
The pushout of $A\leftarrow A\times B\to B$ is the join $A*B$, so $f*g$ is the map $A*B\to*$.
links.why: The join of spaces is the join of maps over a point, so fibrewise statements reduce to the classical join.

reminder: A $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-category is an $n$-category with $k$ tensor products that interchange with each other up to equivalence.
definition: A $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-category is an [$n$-category](c:n-category) with $k$ binary operations on objects that satisfy the [interchange law](c:interchange-law) up to [equivalence](c:equivalence). Formally, it is a $k$-fold delooping: an $(n+k)$-category with exactly one $j$-[morphism](c:k-morphism) for each $j<k$, whose $k$-morphisms are the objects of the $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-category.
examples: For $k=0$ one gets an ordinary $n$-category; for $k=1$ and $n=1$ one gets a monoidal category such as the sets with the cartesian product.
For $k=2$ and $n=1$ one gets braided monoidal categories, and for $k\ge3$ and $n=1$ one gets symmetric monoidal categories.
Non-example: a category with a binary operation on objects that is not a functor is not monoidal, so it is not $k$-tuply monoidal for any $k\ge1$.

steps: Take $n=1$ and $k=1$.
A 1-tuply monoidal 1-category is a 2-category with a single object.
Its 1-morphisms are the objects, its 2-morphisms are the morphisms, and composition of 1-morphisms is the tensor product.
So it is a monoidal category, and every monoidal category arises this way.
links.why: Monoidal categories are the one-object 2-categories, which explains the tensor product as a composition.

steps: Take $n=1$ and $k=2$.
A 2-tuply monoidal 1-category is a 3-category with one object and one 1-morphism.
Its 2-morphisms are the objects, and they compose in two ways that interchange up to a 3-morphism.
The two compositions agree by the Eckmann-Hilton argument, and the interchange 3-morphism is the braiding.
links.why: A braiding appears because the two tensor products collapse into one, up to a coherent equivalence.

reminder: The layer of a finite group is the subgroup generated by all its components.
definition: A component of a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ is a subnormal subgroup $K$ that is [quasisimple](c:quasisimple-group); here subnormal means that $K=K_0\trianglelefteq K_1\trianglelefteq\cdots\trianglelefteq K_m=G$ for some chain of subgroups. A quasisimple group is a perfect [central extension](c:central-extension) of a [simple group](c:simple-group). The layer $E(G)$ is the subgroup generated by all components of $G$; it is a central product of them.
examples: If $G$ is solvable, then $G$ has no components, so $E(G)=1$.
If $G$ is quasisimple, for example $A_5$ or $\mathrm{SL}(2,5)$, then $E(G)=G$.
Non-example: the Fitting subgroup is generated by the nilpotent [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup), so it is not the layer; for $S_5$ it is trivial while the layer is $A_5$.

reminder: The Lelong number of a plurisubharmonic function $\varphi$ at $x$ is $\liminf_{z\to x}\varphi(z)/\log|z-x|$.
definition: Let $\varphi$ be a plurisubharmonic function on an open set of $\mathbb C^n$, and let $x$ be a point. The Lelong number of $\varphi$ at $x$ is $\nu(\varphi,x)=\liminf_{z\to x}\varphi(z)/\log|z-x|=\lim_{r\to0}\max_{|z-x|=r}\varphi(z)/\log r$. For a [closed positive current](c:closed-positive-current) $T=\tfrac{i}{\pi}\partial\bar\partial\varphi$ of type $(1,1)$, the Lelong number of $T$ at $x$ is $\nu(\varphi,x)$.
examples: For $\varphi=\log|z|$ on $\mathbb C^n$, the Lelong number at $0$ is $1$.
For $\varphi=\log|f|$ with $f$ [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function), the Lelong number at $x$ is the vanishing order of $f$ at $x$; for $f=z_1^2+z_2^3$ at $0$ it is $2$.
Non-example: the value $\varphi(x)$ is not the Lelong number; a smooth function has Lelong number $0$ at every point, even where $\varphi(x)\neq0$.

reminder: A Lie subalgebra of a Lie algebra is a submodule that is closed under the Lie bracket.
definition: Let $L$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a ring $R$. A Lie subalgebra of $L$ is a [submodule](c:submodule) $K\subseteq L$ such that $[x,y]\in K$ for all $x,y\in K$. With the restricted bracket, $K$ is itself a Lie algebra.
examples: The trace-zero matrices $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ form a Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$, because $\mathrm{tr}[A,B]=0$.
The strictly upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices form a Lie subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$.
Non-example: in $\mathfrak{gl}_2$, the span of $E_{12}$ and $E_{21}$ is a subspace but not a Lie subalgebra, because $[E_{12},E_{21}]=E_{11}-E_{22}$ lies outside it.

steps: Take a Lie ideal $I$ of $L$, so $[x,y]\in I$ for all $x\in L$ and $y\in I$.
In particular $[x,y]\in I$ for all $x,y\in I$, because $I\subseteq L$.
So $I$ is a submodule closed under the bracket, that is, a Lie subalgebra.
links.why: Ideals are the subalgebras that also absorb brackets with the whole algebra, and this extra condition makes quotient Lie algebras possible.

reminder: A set of vectors is linearly independent when no vector in it is a linear combination of the others.
definition: A subset $S$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ is linearly independent if the only [linear combination](c:linear-combination) $c_1v_1+\dots+c_mv_m$ of distinct vectors $v_i\in S$ that equals $0$ has $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$. Equivalently, no vector of $S$ is a linear combination of the others.
examples: The standard vectors $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are linearly independent in $k^n$.
In the space of polynomials, the set $\{1,x,x^2,\dots\}$ is linearly independent.
Non-example: the set $\{(1,2),(2,4)\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ is linearly dependent, because $2\cdot(1,2)-(2,4)=0$.

steps: Take a basis $B$ of the vector space $V$.
By definition, $B$ is linearly independent.
So every basis is a linearly independent subset; a basis adds the condition that $B$ spans $V$.
links.why: A basis is a linearly independent set that is large enough to span, so independence is half of the definition of a basis.

reminder: The logarithmic counting function of a divisor $D$ sums $D(z)\log(r/|z|)$ over the points $z$ in the disk $|z|\le r$.
definition: Let $D$ be an integer-valued function with [locally finite](c:locally-finite-family) support on $\mathbb C$, such as the divisor of zeros or poles of a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function). Its logarithmic counting function is $N(D,r)=\sum_{0<|z|\le r}D(z)\log\frac{r}{|z|}+D(0)\log r$. It is also called the Nevanlinna counting function, and with the proximity function it gives the [Nevanlinna characteristic](c:nevanlinna-characteristic).
examples: If $D$ has the single value $1$ at a point $a\neq0$, then $N(D,r)=\log(r/|a|)$ for $r\ge|a|$ and $N(D,r)=0$ for $r<|a|$.
For a polynomial $p$ of degree $d$ and the value $0$, the function $N(D,r)$ is $d\log r$ plus a constant for large $r$.
Non-example: the plain counting function $n(r)=\sum_{|z|\le r}D(z)$ counts points without the weight $\log(r/|z|)$, so it is not the logarithmic counting function.

reminder: The logarithmic density of a set $A$ of positive integers is the limit of $\frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{n\in A,n\le x}\frac1n$ as $x\to\infty$.
definition: For a subset $A$ of the [natural numbers](c:natural-number), the logarithmic density is $\delta_{\log}(A)=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{n\in A,\,n\le x}\frac1n$, when this limit exists. The lower and upper logarithmic densities use $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ instead of the limit.
examples: The set of multiples of $d$ has logarithmic density $1/d$.
The set of positive integers with leading decimal digit $1$ has logarithmic density $\log_{10}2$.

Non-example: let $A$ contain the integers in $[e^{4^{2k}},e^{4^{2k+1}})$ for all $k$ and no others. Its lower density is $1/5$ and its upper density is $4/5$, so its logarithmic density does not exist.

reminder: A Mackey functor of a finite group $G$ gives abelian groups $M(H)$ with restriction and transfer maps obeying the double coset formula.
definition: For a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$, a Mackey functor $M$ assigns an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $M(H)$ to each subgroup $H\le G$, with restriction maps $M(K)\to M(H)$ and transfer maps $M(H)\to M(K)$ for $H\le K$, and with conjugation maps. The restriction of a transfer is a sum of transfers of restrictions over double cosets (the double coset formula). Equivalently, $M$ is an [additive functor](c:additive) from the [Burnside category](c:burnside-category) of finite $G$-sets to abelian groups.
examples: Group cohomology $H\mapsto H^n(H;A)$, with restriction and corestriction as transfer, is a Mackey functor.
The Burnside ring functor $H\mapsto A(H)$, where $A(H)$ is the [Burnside ring](c:burnside-ring) of finite $H$-sets, is a Mackey functor.
For a $G$-module $A$, the fixed points $H\mapsto A^H$, with inclusion as restriction and the sum over cosets as transfer, form a Mackey functor.
Non-example: a functor $H\mapsto M(H)$ with restriction maps only has no transfers, so it is not a Mackey functor.

steps: Take a Green functor $R$ for $G$, that is, a Mackey functor with products $R(H)\otimes R(H)\to R(H)$ and units.
Forget the products and the units.
What remains is a Mackey functor, so every Green functor is a Mackey functor.
links.why: Green functors are the Mackey functors with a compatible ring structure, as modules over them are Mackey functors again.

reminder: A binary operation is medial when $(a\cdot b)\cdot(c\cdot d)=(a\cdot c)\cdot(b\cdot d)$ for all $a,b,c,d$.
definition: A [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\cdot$ on a set $A$, which makes $(A,\cdot)$ a magma, is medial if $(a\cdot b)\cdot(c\cdot d)=(a\cdot c)\cdot(b\cdot d)$ for all $a,b,c,d\in A$. By the Eckmann-Hilton argument, a medial magma with a unit is an abelian monoid.
examples: Every commutative semigroup is medial, because associativity and commutativity give $(ab)(cd)=(ac)(bd)$.
The operation $a\ast b=a-b$ on $\mathbb R$ is medial, since $(a-b)-(c-d)=(a-c)-(b-d)$, and it is not associative.
Non-example: the group $S_3$ is not medial, because a medial magma with a unit must be commutative and $S_3$ is not.

reminder: The modified Bernoulli number is $B_n^*=\sum_{r=0}^n\binom{n+r}{2r}\frac{B_r}{n+r}$ for $n\ge1$.
definition: For $n\ge1$, Zagier's modified Bernoulli number is $B_n^*=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n+r}{2r}\frac{B_r}{n+r}$, where $B_r$ are the [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number) with $B_1=-\tfrac12$. It is a rational number built from $B_0,\dots,B_n$. Unlike $B_n$, it is not zero for odd $n\ge3$, and for odd $n$ its value depends only on $n$ modulo $12$.
examples: The first values are $B_1^*=\tfrac34$, $B_2^*=\tfrac1{24}$ and $B_3^*=-\tfrac14$.
For odd $n$ the value $B_n^*$ is $\pm\tfrac14$ or $\pm\tfrac34$; for example $B_5^*=-\tfrac14$ and $B_7^*=\tfrac14$.
Non-example: the ordinary Bernoulli number $B_3$ is $0$, but $B_3^*=-\tfrac14$, so $B_n^*$ is not $B_n$.

reminder: A modular operad has operations indexed by genus and number of legs, composed by gluing legs, including self-gluing that raises genus.
definition: A modular operad is a collection of objects $P((g,n))$ with an $S_n$-action in a symmetric monoidal category, one for each genus $g\ge0$ and number of legs $n\ge0$ with $2g-2+n>0$. It has gluing maps $P((g_1,n_1))\otimes P((g_2,n_2))\to P((g_1+g_2,n_1+n_2-2))$ that join a leg of one operation to a leg of another, and self-gluing maps $P((g,n))\to P((g+1,n-2))$ that join two legs of one operation. These maps are equivariant and associative, as for the sewing of punctured [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface) in an [operad](c:operad) of surfaces.
examples: The homology $H_*(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n})$ of the moduli spaces of stable curves of genus $g$ with $n$ marked points is a modular operad, with gluing of curves at marked points.
Every [cyclic operad](c:cyclic-operad), such as the associative operad, gives a modular operad that is concentrated in genus $0$.
Non-example: a plain operad has no genus and no action that swaps the output with an input, so it is not a modular operad as it stands.

steps: Take a cyclic operad $Q$ in a category with a zero object, with objects $Q(n)$ and $S_{n+1}$-actions.
Set $P((0,n+1))=Q(n)$ and set $P((g,n))=0$ for $g>0$.
Gluing two genus-0 operations gives genus 0, and every gluing that raises the genus lands in the zero object.
So $P$ is a modular operad whose genus-0 part is $Q$.
links.why: Cyclic operads are the genus-0 part of modular operads, so modular operads add the higher-genus gluing.

reminder: A modular representation is a linear representation of a finite group over a field whose characteristic divides the group order.
definition: A modular representation of a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ is a [group representation](c:group-representation) $G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ on a vector space $V$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ of positive [characteristic](c:characteristic) $p$, where $p$ divides $|G|$. In this case Maschke's theorem fails, and a representation need not be a direct sum of irreducible ones.
examples: The regular representation of $\mathbb Z/p$ over $\mathbb F_p$ is modular, and it is not semisimple.
The permutation representation of $S_3$ on $\mathbb F_3^3$ is modular, because $3$ divides $6$; the line spanned by $(1,1,1)$ lies inside the plane of vectors with coordinate sum $0$.
Non-example: a representation of $S_3$ over $\mathbb C$, or over $\mathbb F_5$, is not modular, because the characteristic does not divide $6$.

steps: Take a representation $\rho\colon G\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ of a finite group $G$ over a field $k$.
Add the condition that the characteristic of $k$ is a prime $p$ that divides $|G|$.
Under this condition Maschke's theorem fails, and the representation can have non-split extensions.
links.why: General facts about representations apply, and the divisibility condition marks the case where semisimplicity can fail.

reminder: A module spectrum over a ring spectrum $R$ is a spectrum with an associative, unital action of $R$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring spectrum](c:ring-spectrum). A module spectrum over $R$ is a spectrum $M$ with an action map $R\wedge M\to M$, which uses the [smash product of spectra](c:smash-product-of-spectra), that is associative and unital. Depending on the setting, this holds up to homotopy, strictly in a point-set model, or up to a coherent system of homotopies in the (∞,1)-categorical sense.
examples: Every spectrum is a module over the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum).
A ring spectrum is a module over itself.
Modules over the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $H\mathbb Z$ correspond to chain complexes of abelian groups.
Non-example: a spectrum $M$ whose homotopy groups are modules over the homotopy groups of $R$ is not necessarily a module spectrum, because the action must exist on $M$ itself.

steps: Take a ring $A$ and an $A$-module $M$.
Form the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectra](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $HA$ and $HM$.
The action $A\otimes M\to M$ induces $HA\wedge HM\to HM$, so $HM$ is a module spectrum over $HA$.
links.why: Ordinary modules are the discrete module spectra, so module spectra extend module theory with higher homotopy.

reminder: A Moore space $M(G,n)$ has reduced homology $G$ in degree $n$ and zero in every other degree.
definition: Let $G$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) and $n\ge1$. A Moore space $M(G,n)$ is a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with reduced [homology](c:homology) $\tilde H_n=G$ and $\tilde H_k=0$ for $k\neq n$, which is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) when $n\ge2$. Such a space exists for every $G$ and $n$, and for $n\ge2$ it is unique up to homotopy equivalence.
examples: The space $M(\mathbb Z,n)$ is the sphere $S^n$.
The space $M(\mathbb Z/m,n)$ is $S^n$ with an $(n+1)$-cell attached by a map of degree $m$; for example $M(\mathbb Z/2,1)$ is the real projective plane.
Non-example: the torus $T^2$ has reduced homology $\mathbb Z^2$ in degree 1 and $\mathbb Z$ in degree 2, so it is not a Moore space.

steps: Take $G=\mathbb Z$ and $n\ge1$.
The sphere $S^n$ is a CW complex with $\tilde H_n(S^n)=\mathbb Z$ and no other reduced homology.
For $n\ge2$ the sphere is also simply connected, so $S^n$ is a Moore space $M(\mathbb Z,n)$.
links.why: Spheres are the Moore spaces for the group of integers, and other groups give spaces with torsion homology.

reminder: A morphism of schemes is of finite type when it is quasi-compact and locally given by finitely generated algebras.
definition: A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ of [schemes](c:scheme) is locally of finite type if $Y$ has a cover by [affine](c:affine-scheme) opens $\mathrm{Spec}\,A_i$, and each $f^{-1}(\mathrm{Spec}\,A_i)$ is covered by affine opens $\mathrm{Spec}\,B_{ij}$ with $B_{ij}$ a [finitely generated algebra](c:finitely-generated-algebra) over $A_i$. It is of finite type if it is also [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact); then each such preimage needs only finitely many $\mathrm{Spec}\,B_{ij}$.
examples: The affine space $\mathrm{Spec}\,A[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is of finite type.
A closed immersion $\mathrm{Spec}\,A/I\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is of finite type, because $A/I$ is generated by $1$ as an $A$-algebra.
Non-example: the morphism $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb Q\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb Z$ is not of finite type, because $\mathbb Q$ is not a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra.

steps: Take a closed immersion $Z\to Y$; over an affine $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\subseteq Y$ it is $\mathrm{Spec}\,A/I\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$.
The quotient $A/I$ is generated as an $A$-algebra by the single element $1$.
Closed immersions are affine, hence quasi-compact, so the closed immersion is of finite type.
links.why: Closed immersions are the finite type morphisms that are also closed embeddings, so finite type results apply to them.

reminder: An $n$-category has objects and $k$-morphisms up to dimension $n$, with composition that is associative and unital up to coherent equivalence.
definition: An $n$-category, for $n\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$, has objects, 1-morphisms between objects, and so on up to $n$-morphisms between $(n-1)$-morphisms, with composition at every level that is associative and unital. This holds strictly or up to coherent higher [equivalence](c:equivalence), depending on the model, and the [$k$-morphisms](c:k-morphism) for $k>n$ are trivial.
examples: An ordinary [category](c:category) is a 1-category, and a set is a 0-category.
The category of small categories, with functors and natural transformations, is a [2-category](c:2-category).
For a space $X$, the fundamental $n$-groupoid has points as objects, paths as 1-morphisms, homotopies as 2-morphisms, and so on.
Non-example: a directed graph has objects and arrows but no composition, so it is not an $n$-category for any $n$.

steps: Take the case $n=1$ of an $n$-category.
A 1-category has objects and 1-morphisms and nothing above them, with associative and unital composition.
These are the axioms of an ordinary category, so a 1-category is exactly a category.
links.why: Ordinary category theory is the case $n=1$ of the theory of $n$-categories.

steps: Take the case $n=2$ of an $n$-category.
A 2-category has objects, 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms, with composition in each dimension and the interchange law.
These are the axioms of a 2-category, so the case $n=2$ is exactly 2-categories.
links.why: Two-dimensional category theory is the case $n=2$ of the theory of $n$-categories.
